name: C++
year_note: Bjarne Stroustrup started 'C with Classes' at Bell Labs in 1979; it was renamed C++ in 1983 and released commercially (Cfront 1.0), together with the first edition of 'The C++ Programming Language', in October 1985.
tagline: C plus zero-overhead abstractions: classes, templates and RAII on top of C's machine model.
summary: C++ extends C with classes, templates, exceptions and deterministic destruction (RAII), aiming for abstractions that cost nothing at run time compared with hand-written code. It is a multi-paradigm systems language used for operating systems, browsers, game engines, databases, finance and high-performance computing. Standardized by ISO since 1998, it has been revised every three years since C++11.
history:
Bjarne Stroustrup began 'C with Classes' at Bell Labs in 1979, wanting the program-organization facilities of Simula — which he had found productive but too slow during his PhD work at Cambridge — combined with the speed and portability of C. Classes, derived classes, access control and inline functions were implemented by the Cfront front end, which translated to C. Renamed C++ in 1983 (a name suggested by Rick Mascitti), the language was released commercially in October 1985 alongside the first edition of 'The C++ Programming Language'.

Release 2.0 (1989) added multiple inheritance and abstract classes, and the Annotated C++ Reference Manual (1990) specified templates and exception handling. The first ISO standard, C++98, incorporated Alexander Stepanov's Standard Template Library, making generic programming with templates a central style of the language.

C++11 modernized the language with auto, lambdas, move semantics, smart pointers and a memory model for threads, and the committee has since shipped a revision every three years: C++14, C++17, C++20 (concepts, ranges, coroutines, modules) and C++23. Contracts and static reflection have been voted into the working draft for C++26.
innovations: Zero-overhead abstraction: classes, inlining and templates that compile to code as efficient as hand-written C
RAII: tying resource lifetime to object scope through constructors and destructors
Templates and the STL made generic programming and compile-time metaprogramming mainstream
Brought Simula-style object-oriented programming to mainstream systems programming
User-defined types that behave like built-ins via operator overloading, references and value semantics

typing.notes: Stronger than C (no implicit void* conversion, type-safe linkage), but C's implicit numeric conversions and unchecked casts remain. `auto` and template argument deduction infer types locally; templates are checked structurally at instantiation.

influenced_by.note: Designed as a (nearly) compatible superset of C, keeping its syntax, types and machine model.
Classes, derived classes and virtual functions came from Simula 67.
Operator overloading and declarations anywhere in a block.
Generics and exceptions informed the design of templates and exception handling.

influenced_by_external.name: Mesa
influenced_by_external.note: Listed among C++'s influences (exceptions and modularity).

exceptions.note: try/catch/throw, specified in the Annotated C++ Reference Manual (1990) and standardized in C++98; destructors run during unwinding.

coroutines.note: Stackless coroutines via co_await/co_yield/co_return; the standard library offers few ready-made coroutine types.

generators.note: std::generator built on C++20 coroutines; STL iterators and C++20 range views are the classic alternative.

type-inference.note: `auto`, `decltype` and template argument deduction; no global inference.

generics.note: Templates (specified in the 1990 ARM, first shipped in Cfront 3.0); the STL joined the standard in C++98, and C++20 concepts constrain template parameters.

algebraic-data-types.note: std::variant, std::optional and std::tuple; matching is done with std::visit rather than language syntax.

type-classes.note: Concepts name sets of requirements on types, but types satisfy them implicitly rather than by declaring instances.

option-types.note: std::optional; raw pointers can still be null, so there is no null safety.

structural-typing.note: Templates are 'duck-typed' at compile time: any type with the required operations works. Class types are otherwise nominal.

ownership.note: Move semantics and std::unique_ptr express unique ownership, but borrowing and lifetimes are not checked by the compiler.

interfaces.note: Abstract classes with pure virtual functions serve as interfaces; there is no separate interface construct.

inheritance.note: Multiple inheritance (since 2.0, 1989) and virtual base classes.

traits-mixins.note: Mixins via multiple inheritance and the CRTP idiom.

abstract-data-types.note: private/protected members hide a class's representation.

modules.note: Traditionally header files, separate compilation and namespaces; C++20 modules are still being adopted by toolchains.

first-class-functions.note: Lambdas and std::function; function pointers and function objects before that.

closures.note: Lambdas capture by value or by reference through explicit capture lists.

immutability.note: `const` and `constexpr`, but mutability is the default.

lazy-evaluation.note: Range views are evaluated lazily; the language itself is strict.

pointers.note: Raw pointers and pointer arithmetic from C, plus references and smart pointers.

async-await.note: co_await transforms functions into state machines, but task and executor types come from libraries.

reflection.note: Only run-time type information (typeid, dynamic_cast) in C++23; compile-time static reflection has been voted into C++26.

compile-time-execution.note: constexpr functions (much extended in C++14/20, plus consteval) on top of template metaprogramming, which dates from the 1990s.

milestones.event: Stroustrup begins 'C with Classes' at Bell Labs
Cfront 1.0 and 'The C++ Programming Language' (1st edition)
The Annotated C++ Reference Manual specifies templates and exceptions
C++98, the first ISO standard, including the STL
C++11: auto, lambdas, move semantics, smart pointers, threads
Contracts and static reflection voted into the C++26 draft

trivia: The name C++ was suggested by Rick Mascitti in 1983; Mascitti later said it was given 'in a tongue-in-cheek spirit', after C's ++ increment operator.
Stroustrup's motivation came from his Cambridge PhD work, where he found Simula well suited to large programs but too slow for practical use.

hello.notes: `std::cout << ...` is itself operator overloading on a stream object. C++23 also offers std::println (GCC 14+).

factorial.notes: `constexpr` lets the same function run at compile time (checked by static_assert) or at run time.

higher-order.notes: C++20 range views compose lazily with `|`; nothing is computed until the for loop pulls values.

shapes.notes: Classic OOP: an abstract base class, virtual dispatch and std::unique_ptr ownership. std::variant with std::visit (C++17) is the closed sum-type alternative.

signature.title: RAII: destructors that always run
signature.expected_output:
open log.txt
open db
close db
close log.txt
caught: disk full
signature.notes: When the exception leaves work(), destructors run in reverse order of construction. This deterministic cleanup is how C++ manages files, locks and memory (std::unique_ptr, std::lock_guard) without a garbage collector.
